payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.

parsed.text:
The graph’s main flaw is that it turns the broad request into unsupported coverage requirements: “both giraffes and the background” must each read as chalk-rendered. The source image does contain two giraffes, but the instruction does not require every subject or the background to be independently transformed. Remove those conjunctive conditions from the outcome target, reference, and completion/partial criteria. Judge whether the edited image as a whole has become a chalk drawing, using the source only to assess the requested transformation—not to impose a per-region checklist.

Keep the distinction between a genuine medium transformation and a superficial texture overlay, but make it an overall-impression test rather than requiring a particular technique or uniform treatment. The edited image has a strong grainy, softened, sketch-like appearance across the scene, while retaining recognizable giraffe forms and pattern detail. The criteria should let the evaluator weigh those cues together: visible chalk-like treatment is evidence of progress, while completion depends on whether the overall result convincingly reads as a chalk drawing. Do not prescribe the reference label or treat retained detail alone as disqualifying.

Preserve R1’s ID, text, and exact source quote. The existing single requested check covers the sole requirement, so no extra requirement or support check is needed; revise its criteria and the outcome’s target/reference to remove the invented subject-and-background coverage test while retaining clear complete, partial, absent, and genuinely insufficient-evidence distinctions.
